newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish rate rise seen priced in Warsaw shares.
newsitem.headline: Polish rate rise seen priced in Warsaw shares.

text.p: The Polish bourse could fall on Monday after Friday's interest rate rise by the central bank but analysts said market downside was limited as the news had already been largely priced in.
"The market could fall a little on Monday, but not too much, because to a large degree the fact has already been discounted," said Pawel Tarnowski, an analyst at Raiffeisen Capital & Investment.

"To a certain degree it's a positive thing because it shows that the NBP (the central bank) is trying to handle the situation on the money market. After the money supply growth we've had, worse would be if there was no rate rise," he added.
On Friday the central bank said it would increase on August 4 the lombard rate by two points to 27 percent and the discount rate by 2.5 points to 24.5 percent.
Poland's broad money rose by 4.88 billion zlotys ($1.4 billion), or 3.2 percent, in the first 20 days of July to 156.04 billion zlotys after a two-percent rise in June.
The main market's all-share WIG index rose 0.4 percent this week to 15,116.8 points.

Analysts said an interest-rate rise had already been expected in part due to the flooding that hit the southwest of the country last month, for which the government might borrow as much as 2.5 billion zlotys from the central bank.

The rate rise seemed all but done on Wednesday when the bank's president said in a newspaper that nominal rates must go up, and analysts said recent falls in stock prices also helped suggest the bourse had used up most of its downward potential.

"The market has fallen pretty strongly in the past half year and I think more falls would have to be generated by something -- 15,000 points seems to be holding," said Artur Kobos, a trader at ING Barings in Warsaw.
Analysts said there could even be a rise next week despite the rate rise but overall they saw little upside in the run-up to the parliamentary elections due on September 21.
Among large-cap stocks the main story of the week was Budimex, which tumbled 25.4 percent after last Friday's 10-percent plunge on the news it had revised down its 1997 profit forecast.
Analysts said Polifarb Wroclaw, suspended from bourse trade since July 11 due to flooding, should fall on Monday, when it resumes trade without the daily 10-percent price fluctuation limit.
The firm incurred 11.6 million zlotys in damage and lowered its 1997 net profit forecast by 10.2 percent.
